article.title: Studying an emerging sign language won't kill it – so what are linguists scared of?
article.outlet: Aeon (republished by the World Economic Forum)
article.summary: Michael Erard looks at 'village sign languages', which are new languages that appear in small, isolated communities with many deaf members. The piece is about a debate among linguists. Some worry that studying these young languages could harm them. Others think they should be treated as full languages and compared with other sign languages straight away. Along the way it visits places such as a Turkish village, a Japanese island and a Mexican community.
facts: Researcher Connie de Vos has deaf relatives in a Turkish village. They invented a sign language that everyone around them used to communicate with them.
Some 'universals' of sign languages turned out not to be universal once village sign languages were studied.
On an island in Japan, a signer says the locals think little about their own Miyakubo Sign Language.
Researchers in Oaxaca, Mexico, found that a signer who knew ASL accidentally brought some ASL features into her Chatino signing.
questions: If studying a young language could change it, how should researchers balance curiosity against protecting it?
Why might the way a language is passed on, through a family or through a school, change how it develops?
What would count as proof that a feature of language is truly universal?

related.t: New sign languages hint at how all languages evolve
Deaf Arab villagers create new language

alt.title: Bali's remarkable deaf village
alt.summary: This feature visits Bengkala, a Balinese village with a high rate of hereditary deafness. There, a local sign language called Kata Kolok is the main way a small number of deaf people communicate. Many hearing villagers have learned it too, so deaf people take part fully in village life. The language has grown naturally and has little in common with other sign languages.
facts: Kata Kolok means 'deaf talk', and the article says it is the main language for only 44 people.
More than half of the hearing people in the village have learned it so they can talk with deaf relatives and friends.
The sign for 'male' is a stiff pointing index finger. 'Father' uses the same finger curved over the upper lip like a moustache.
A researcher who is fluent in it says it has very little influence from Indonesian, Balinese or outside sign languages.
questions: What does it say about a community when hearing people learn the language of their deaf neighbours?
Why might a language used by so few people still count as rich and complete?
What could be lost if a village sign language gives way to a national one?

related.t: Longitudinal Documentation of Sign Language Acquisition in a Deaf Village in Bali
The Emergence of Language in Social Interaction (CORDIS project report)
Vital Signs: In Bali's 'deaf village,' a unique language gives hope to a new generation

article.title: Ancient Greeks Voted to Kick Politicians Out of Athens if Enough People Didn't Like Them
article.summary: In Athens, citizens could vote to send a powerful figure into exile without a trial. They did it by scratching a name onto a broken piece of pottery called an ostrakon. The article explains how thousands of these ballots, found by archaeologists, show how voters behaved and fill gaps left by ancient writers. The ballots also show that some exiled politicians came back and were ostracized again.
facts: Ostracism ran from about 487 to 416 B.C., and it let citizens banish someone without a trial.
The first ostrakon was identified in 1853, and only about 1,600 had been counted over the next century.
A German team started finding thousands more in Athens' Kerameikos pottery district in 1966.
Evidence from the ballots led archaeologists to conclude that Megakles returned to Athens and was ostracized again in 471 B.C.
questions: Is voting someone out without a trial a useful check on power, or a risky tool? Why?
What can discarded everyday objects like pottery scraps tell us about how ordinary voters behaved that official histories leave out?
Which modern procedures, such as recalls or impeachments, do something similar to ostracism, and how do they differ?

related.t: Ostracism: Political Exclusion in Ancient Athens (World History Encyclopedia)
Ostracism: 'Cancel culture' Ancient Greek-style (History Hit / History.co.uk)

alt.title: The Dogal Elections Edition
alt.summary: Venice chose its head of state, the doge, with rules adopted in 1268 that stayed almost unchanged until the last election in 1789. The process used repeated rounds of drawing lots and then voting. It shrank a large pool of nobles down to 41 electors, who needed 25 votes to elect the doge. The newsletter asks why the system was so convoluted and why it lasted so long. It suggests that combining chance with an isolated electoral college makes manipulation harder and encourages careful deliberation.
facts: Venice used its doge-election rules from 1268 until the Republic fell in 1797, and the process had ten rounds that alternated lot and vote.
The odd number 41 came from a failed election in 1229. A tie in a college of forty was settled by drawing lots, and the rules were then changed to make the final college odd.
Before 1268, seven of 43 doges came from the previous doge's family, and in six of those cases the office passed from father to son.
Because the doge served for life and was usually elected at an advanced age, the office was kept from becoming too powerful.
questions: Why might a deliberately complicated voting process make an election more trusted instead of less?
What are the trade-offs of picking decision-makers partly by chance rather than purely by votes?
Which modern institutions use lotteries or multi-stage selection, and would you want to see more of them?

related.t: The Early History of Approval Voting (Center for Election Science)
How the Republic of Venice chose its Doge: lot-based elections and supermajority rule (Constitutional Political Economy, Springer)

article.title: A Mysterious Wasteland
article.summary: In 1960 a Soviet scientist driving through the southern Urals found a huge stretch of empty, contaminated land. The article follows the detective work that tried to explain it. An exiled biologist combed open Soviet scientific journals for clues, and Western experts first doubted his claim that buried nuclear waste had overheated and erupted. Later surveys confirmed a devastated zone, but people kept arguing over what caused it.
facts: The traveler, Lev Tumerman, passed a road sign telling drivers not to stop for the next 20 miles and to go as fast as possible.
The contamination was traced to the winter of 1957-58, around Kyshtym, which was believed to be a center of Soviet plutonium production.
The exiled biologist Zhores Medvedev proposed that stored radioactive waste overheated as it built up and then blew up like a volcano.
Authorities reportedly sent prisoners to cover the contaminated soil with sand, and later evacuated farmers, destroyed their houses and fenced the area off.
questions: How can scientists reconstruct a hidden pollution event from indirect evidence, such as open journals and a single eyewitness?
Why might governments hide environmental disasters, and what is lost when they do?
What does this case suggest about how much we should trust a surprising claim when the official data is missing?

related.t: LA-9217-MS: An analysis of the Kyshtym claims (Los Alamos report)

alt.title: Chemists are uncovering a hidden world of pollution
alt.summary: Salmon were dying and no one knew what was killing them. The article shows how chemists solved that puzzle and why the same method is now revealing many more pollutants. Modern high-resolution instruments paired with computer analysis can pick out thousands of compounds in one sample, including ones nobody thought to look for. The salmon case ended with the discovery of a tire-derived chemical, which set off a continuing legal and regulatory fight.
facts: The unknown compound was matched to an obscure 1983 paper about a related tire additive called 6PPD.
When researchers exposed 6PPD to ozone, as happens to tire debris on roads, they made the mystery compound, which they named 6PPD-quinone.
For decades, scientists mostly measured only the contaminants they already knew to look for, by comparing samples with reference standards.
In 2023, two fishing industry groups sued 13 tire manufacturers over the chemical.
questions: If we can only find the pollutants we think to look for, how many others might be affecting ecosystems right now?
Who should pay for harm caused by a chemical that was added to a product for a good reason, such as keeping tires from cracking?
How does a chemical change once it leaves the factory and meets sunlight, air and roads?

related.t: A Fish Kill Mystery (Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution archive)
Four Big Pollution Diseases of Japan (Wikipedia)

article.title: AI before AI: The forgotten Soviet programme (1/3)
article.summary: Silicon Valley dominates the usual story of artificial intelligence. This piece looks at the Soviet effort that began in the 1950s, which gets far less attention. Researchers behind the Iron Curtain first approached the idea through cybernetics, and AI itself was treated with suspicion at the start. The article follows how the field grew into an organised research community, and how one Soviet-born idea later found its way into a company and a connection to Apple.
facts: In the early 1950s, Soviet authorities viewed the ideas behind AI with suspicion, and the field was not yet called AI.
Soviet researchers came to machine intelligence through cybernetics, the study of how humans and machines, or machines and other machines, behave.
A Russian Association for Artificial Intelligence was founded in 1989 after years of lobbying and community-building.
A solution by a Soviet researcher named Guberman was picked up by entrepreneur Stepan Pachikov for his company Paragraph.
questions: Why might a political system distrust a new field of science at first, and then later embrace it?
How does the story of AI change if we count work done outside the United States and Britain?
What other 'forgotten' technology stories might be hiding behind national borders or political divides?

related.t: The birth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) research

alt.title: Science: The Thinking Machine
alt.summary: This is a TIME magazine piece from January 1950, written when the idea of a 'thinking machine' was brand new. It introduces Harvard's early computers, including a glass-sided veteran nicknamed Bessie, and describes how they answer hard technical questions. It contrasts these machines with a plain adding machine, and with the human brain, whose memory they can't yet match. It is a snapshot of how the press talked about machine intelligence before the term 'artificial intelligence' existed.
facts: Bessie, a machine with 760,000 parts, had been working since 1944.
Harvard's Mark III stored its memory on fast-spinning aluminum cylinders coated with magnetic material.
The Mark III was meant for ambitious jobs such as long-range weather forecasting, and the Navy was due to receive it.
The article calls Bessie a sort of 'mechanical Eve' for later machines, even though she was far from the brightest.
questions: What did people in 1950 mean by a 'thinking machine', and how does that differ from what we mean by AI today?
Why do you think early writers kept describing computers in human or animal terms, like giving them names and genders?
If machines in 1950 could already forecast weather in theory, what might they have been missing that made true 'thinking' hard?

related.t: Thinking Machine, Astounding Science Fiction cover
The birth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) research
